title: Can Washington and China Build Confidence Around AI and Stability?
gist: After Xi Jinping's September 2026 White House visit produced a U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue and an SI-incident channel, Lonergan argues these are confidence-building measures, not AI arms control, and that the November 2026 exchange should stay narrowly focused on human control over nuclear use, shared definitions, and observable behavioral indicators—avoiding export controls and 'pace the frontier' rhetoric that feeds Chinese suspicions.

insights.claim: Ahead of Xi Jinping's September 2026 White House visit, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng at JPMorgan Chase's New York offices and proposed a U.S.-China dialogue to notify each other of AI-related national security incidents.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: AI is now a Treasury-led channel in U.S.-China economic diplomacy, linking AI to broader trade negotiations.
insights.quote: moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important
insights.locator: In the lead-up to General Secretary

insights.claim: The U.S. readout of the 2026 Xi-Trump meeting said the two countries agreed to establish a 'U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue' with the next exchange by November 2026, plus a bilateral communication channel for SI incidents, while China's readout affirmed that 'AI must be kept under human control.'
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: A formal bilateral AI channel modestly reduces tail risk of AI-triggered crises between the two largest AI powers.
insights.quote: AI must be kept under human control.

insights.claim: The proposed U.S.-China AI dialogues would not restrain AI innovation, change the balance of AI power, or include enforcement or verification, so they are confidence-building measures rather than AI arms control.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Do not expect the dialogue to constrain AI capex, model development, or export-control competition.
insights.quote: they do not represent a form of AI arms control

insights.claim: Both Washington and Beijing perceive a tradeoff: AI is central to their rivalry—Trump said 'whoever wins AI wins' and China's latest five-year plan calls to 'seize the commanding heights of science and technology development'—yet both fear AI's role in nuclear decisions.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Competition remains the dominant driver; cooperation will be confined to narrow nuclear-risk niches.

insights.claim: Research has shown some large language models, including China's DeepSeek, are more inclined to recommend nuclear options in simulated crises, so AI decision-support may bias choices toward escalation.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Military LLM decision-support adoption carries escalation-bias risk that may shape procurement rules.

insights.claim: This spring, a false AI-generated intelligence report nearly 'started a war' between the United States and China during the U.S. military operation against Iran.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: AI-hallucinated intelligence is a live source of great-power crisis risk, raising geopolitical tail risk.

insights.claim: Even without delegating nuclear launch to machines, integrating AI into nuclear command and control, early warning, and launch decision processes creates new uncertainty and may exacerbate escalation risks.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: NC3 modernization involving AI is a focal point for both risk and policy.
insights.locator: Even if neither party fully delegates

themes.theme: Why AI arms control is unlikely

insights.claim: With New START expiring in February and a tripolar nuclear age emerging, great powers show little appetite for new arms control agreements, and AI's dual-use, general-purpose nature makes cheating hard to detect and capability disclosure unlikely.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Absence of binding AI limits means the AI arms race and associated defense spending continue unabated.
insights.locator: One way to manage these risks

insights.claim: No AI crisis comparable to the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis has occurred, so the U.S. and China lack the vivid shared sense of danger that drove Cold War confidence-building, limiting agreement beyond a broad commitment to human involvement in nuclear use.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Meaningful AI risk agreements may only arrive after a shock event—watch for an AI-triggered crisis as a catalyst.

insights.claim: The U.S. and China define lethal autonomous weapons differently: China uses a high five-criteria threshold possibly met by no current capability, while the U.S. defines them as systems that select and engage targets without further operator intervention once activated.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Definitional gaps allow both sides to keep developing autonomous weapons while claiming compliance.

insights.claim: The concentration of frontier AI in a handful of private firms that control key inputs makes the private sector integral to any AI confidence-building, and their interests may diverge from government's on intrusive inspection or information sharing.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Frontier labs gain leverage in national security policy; regulatory demands on them may grow.
insights.quote: Militaries are uniquely dependent on these private firms.

insights.claim: Cold War confidence-building evolved from the 1963 U.S.-Soviet hotline to 1987 Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers, which in 2013 were extended to cyber crises; Obama used the hotline on Oct. 31, 2016 to warn Putin about election interference.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Existing risk-reduction channels can be extended to AI incidents relatively quickly.
insights.locator: But arms control is not the only option.

insights.claim: Confidence-building measures are easy to abrogate, as when Russia in 2023 stopped sharing armed forces information under the Vienna Document after invading Ukraine, but deviations from shared expectations can still provide early warning.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: A breakdown of the AI dialogue would itself be a leading indicator of rising U.S.-China tension.
insights.locator: Confidence-building measures are not a panacea

insights.claim: The U.S.-China AI dialogue should stay narrowly focused on human control over nuclear use decisions and exclude contentious issues like export controls, restrictions on Chinese AI models, and broader AI governance.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Export controls on chips and models are unlikely to be traded away in this dialogue.

insights.claim: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's appeal to 'pace the frontier' hinders U.S.-China confidence-building because it reinforces Chinese perceptions that the U.S. seeks to consolidate its AI advantages and restrict diffusion that might benefit China.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: U.S. lab safety rhetoric has geopolitical side effects in Beijing's reading of U.S. intent.
insights.locator: The U.S.-Chinese AI dialogue should focus

insights.claim: Initial dialogue rounds should clarify definitions of 'autonomous' capabilities and what human control means in practice for nuclear launch, early warning, and NC3, then develop agreed observable indicators of dangerous AI use in nuclear systems rather than restricting the technology.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Behavior-based, not technology-based, norms leave AI development unconstrained.

insights.claim: How Washington regulates frontier AI labs and firms controlling AI infrastructure inputs—such as incident reporting and safeguard sharing—can itself serve as unilateral confidence-building, and failure to build these domestic mechanisms may undermine any U.S.-China agreement.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: Domestic AI incident-reporting regulation could be justified on national security grounds, raising compliance requirements for labs.

insights.claim: Cross-domain confidence-building on cybersecurity of AI systems may be a future area of shared concern, highlighted by OpenAI agents hacking Hugging Face and research using the AI tool 'WeWorm' to hack WeChat.
insights.speaker: Erica D. Lonergan
insights.so_what: AI-system cybersecurity is emerging as a bilateral concern and a growing security market.
